note: Berkshire presents its balance sheet and income statement as stacked segment columns — Insurance and Other, Railroad Utilities and Energy, and (through 2017) Finance and Financial Products — so most of what matters about it is dimensional and therefore invisible to companyfacts. That is the entire reason its insurance and debt lines came back empty.

metrics.label: Notes payable — Insurance and Other
metrics.note: Borrowings at the parent and the insurance/other subsidiaries. This is the part of consolidated debt that is genuinely Berkshire's own obligation.

metrics.label: Notes payable — Railroad, Utilities and Energy
metrics.note: BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy borrowings. Berkshire states in its 10-K that it 'does not guarantee the repayment of debt issued by BNSF, BHE or any of their subsidiaries' — this is the NON-RECOURSE portion.

metrics.label: Notes payable — Finance and Financial Products
metrics.note: Reported as its own segment column through FY2017 only; from FY2018 these businesses sit inside the other columns, so the series ends rather than going to zero.

metrics.label: Total notes payable and other borrowings
metrics.note: Sum of the segment columns from FY2018 on. Deliberately NOT bound to a single consolidated element: Berkshire does not print one, and inventing it by picking whichever debt-ish tag exists is how the old mapping produced numbers that were off by a factor of twenty.

metrics.label: Recourse debt / total debt
metrics.note: The share of consolidated borrowings Berkshire actually stands behind. Every consolidated leverage ratio for Berkshire overstates holding-company leverage by roughly the inverse of this.

metrics.label: Investment gains (losses)
metrics.note: From 2018 this carries unrealized marks on the equity portfolio (ASU 2016-01) and is the reason reported net income swings by tens of billions.

metrics.label: Net earnings excluding investment gains
metrics.note: A pre-tax-gains subtraction from two reported lines, NOT Berkshire's own operating earnings figure — its published number nets tax on the gains and differs. Berkshire's own figure is text-only in MD&A and is carried separately in company_templates/BRK-B.json.

metrics.label: Short-term Investments (U.S. T-Bills)
metrics.note: Berkshire's T-bill pile is a company extension tag under the insurance segment column, so companyfacts cannot see it.

metrics.label: Cash & Cash Equivalents — Insurance and Other
metrics.note: Berkshire prints cash per segment column and no consolidated line; the insurance-and-other column is the holding-company pile that matters.

metrics.label: Cash & Cash Equivalents — Railroad, Utilities and Energy
Cash & Cash Equivalents
metrics.note: Sum across segment columns — Berkshire tags no consolidated cash line either. The prior binding used the insurance-and-other column alone (~$47.7B in FY2025), understating consolidated cash by the ~$3-4B the railroad/utilities/energy segment holds every year, which fed directly into an understated cash deduction in UNTA.

metrics.label: Investments in equity securities
metrics.note: The marketable equity portfolio (Apple, Coca-Cola, American Express and the rest) as carried on the consolidated balance sheet. Two elements because ASU 2016-01 moved these off available-for-sale accounting: AvailableForSaleSecuritiesEquitySecurities runs through FY2017 and EquitySecuritiesFvNi from FY2017 on, and both print $170.5B in the overlap year, so the series joins cleanly. Ordered alternatives, first match wins, so the newer element takes FY2017+ automatically. Both are bound at the consolidated level (no dimension) rather than the Insurance and Other column, which excludes the ~$0.4-6B held in the other segment columns.

metrics.label: Other Intangible Assets — Insurance and Other
Other Intangible Assets — Railroad, Utilities and Energy
metrics.note: Broken out only for FY2020-FY2021; small (~$1.2B) relative to the insurance segment's $30-36B.

metrics.label: Total Other Intangible Assets
metrics.note: Sum across segment columns. Berkshire tags no consolidated intangibles line, same as debt; binding only the insurance-segment figure understated total intangibles (and therefore overstated tangible equity and every ratio built on it) in the two years the railroad/utilities/energy segment carried its own intangibles balance.

metrics.label: Property, plant and equipment — Insurance and Other
metrics.note: The manufacturing, service and retailing businesses' fixed assets. Dimensional, so invisible to companyfacts — which is why the global ppe_net binding found nothing for Berkshire and the row came back empty.

metrics.label: Property, plant and equipment — Railroad, Utilities and Energy
metrics.note: BNSF's track and rolling stock plus Berkshire Hathaway Energy's generation and transmission plant. By far the larger share — $184.7B of the $216.6B consolidated total in FY2025 — and the reason an empty PP&E row understated Berkshire's fixed-asset base by more than any other single omission on the page.

metrics.label: Property, plant and equipment
metrics.note:
Sum of the two segment columns, matching exactly the lines Berkshire captions 'Property, plant and equipment'. Built the same way as total_debt above and for the same reason: Berkshire prints no consolidated PP&E figure anywhere, so the alternative to summing the columns it does print is an empty row.

Deliberately excludes two neighbouring lines. 'Equipment held for lease' (us-gaap:PropertySubjectToOrAvailableForOperatingLeaseNet, $18.5B in FY2025) is a separate caption on the face of the balance sheet — XTRA and CORT lease inventory, not plant in operating use. The Finance and Financial Products column's 'Property, plant and equipment and assets held for lease' (2013-2017) is that same equipment under the older segment presentation: the two overlap in FY2017 at $9.9B and $10.2B, confirming they are the same assets renamed rather than a gap to fill. Including either would put two captions in one row; excluding both gives a smooth series that grows every year from $100.4B in FY2011 to $216.6B in FY2025.

metrics.label: Interest Expense — Railroad, Utilities and Energy
Interest Expense — Finance and Financial Products
metrics.note: Reported as its own segment column through FY2017 only.

metrics.label: Interest Expense
metrics.note: Sum across segment columns for every year, rather than the consolidated tag where one exists (2013 on) and a fallback to a single segment otherwise (the prior binding). The segment sum ties exactly to the consolidated tag in 13 of 15 years; it runs about $400M (~10%) above the consolidated figure in FY2016-FY2017 specifically, which looks like a cross-filing restatement-timing artifact around the Finance-and-Financial-Products segment's 2018 wind-down rather than a real gap. Using one formula for the whole history was judged better than switching sources mid-series.

metrics.label: Unlevered Net Tangible Assets
metrics.expr: equity + total_debt - total_cash - goodwill - intangibles - equity_securities
metrics.note: The app's standard formula (Equity + Total Debt - Total Cash - Goodwill - Intangibles) with one Berkshire-specific deduction: the marketable equity portfolio. UNTA is meant to isolate the tangible capital the OPERATING businesses run on, and a $300B stake in Apple and Coca-Cola is a financial asset by exactly the same logic that removes cash - it earns a market return, not an operating one. Leaving it in inflated the denominator by roughly the size of the portfolio and pushed Economic Goodwill (NOPAT / UNTA) down to a figure that described the stock market more than the businesses. An earlier version of this override used Total Assets - Goodwill - Intangibles - Total Debt, which subtracted debt with the wrong sign and omitted cash entirely, overstating UNTA (FY2025: $976B vs $360B before this deduction).

metrics.label: Float / Equity
metrics.note: How much investable policyholder money Berkshire runs per dollar of its own capital — the leverage that actually matters here, and the one no debt ratio captures.
